title: POC Weekly — Stream & TTFT Kernel Assign Review
summary: Weekly POC sync to review latest TTFT and streaming results, decide kernel assignment for seqlen buckets, and agree next steps for a 2-week tuning sprint. Discussed KV/prefix caching artifacts, microburst hedging, and a proposed canary plan for dedicated nodes. Action items captured for benchmark artifacts, kernel matrix, and VPC security checklist.
action_items: Maya: Share consolidated CSV of last 3 runs + per-shard TTFT percentiles (due 2026-04-18)
Ravi: Produce kernel-decision matrix with recommended kernels per seqlen bucket and fallback (due 2026-04-20)
Priya: Re-run 1k-request microburst test capturing NVTX traces and upload to share (due 2026-04-19)
Jonah: Provide network egress baseline from ParcelWave VPC to Redwood region (due 2026-04-21)
Maya: Send security checklist + short SSO/SAML note for pilot (due 2026-04-20)
next_steps: Redwood to propose kernel assignments and a canary schedule
ParcelWave to run the microburst NVTX trace test and share results
Schedule 30-min follow-up on 2026-04-22 to confirm canary start
transcript:
Header: 2026-04-16 15:00 PDT | Duration: 44m | Recording: Yes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Ravi Patel (Redwood SE), Hannah Lee (Redwood SE), Amir Costa (ParcelWave - CTO), Priya Singh (ParcelWave - ML Eng), Jonah Price (ParcelWave - SRE), Leah Ortiz (ParcelWave - Product)

Summary (auto): quick review of recent TTFT runs, discuss kernel choices by seqlen, plan microburst hedging and canary for dedicated nodes, assign owners.

[00:00] Maya (Redwood): Hey everyone, thanks for making time. Quick roll call?
[00:05] Amir (ParcelWave): Amir here.
[00:07] Priya (ParcelWave): Priya.
[00:09] Jonah (ParcelWave): Jonah.
[00:11] Leah (ParcelWave): Leah on.
[00:14] Maya: Great. Ravi, Hannah, you good?
[00:16] Ravi (Redwood): Yep. Morning / afternoon all. Real quick agenda — we wanted to walk through last week's TTFT numbers, then the streaming handshake oddities Priya found, and then propose kernels split by seqlen.
[00:28] Priya: I'll jump in on the streaming stuff when you get there. First, on the TTFT numbers we saw the 95th hit about 280ms in the baseline but with microbursts it spiked to 720 on a handful of samples, which is worrying given ParcelWave SLA target is 350ms.
[00:45] Maya: Right. The baseline runs we did with the prefix cache turned on gave us median around 110ms, but worst-case microburst shows big variance. We need to decide whether to favor the lower median or prioritize tail.
[01:05] Ravi: A few notes — our kernel candidates behave differently by seqlen. For seqlen < 256 the fused-attn kernel gives great latency, but it's less stable on request-churn; the stable path is the tiled-kernel which has slightly higher median but better 95/99.
[01:30] Priya: When you say "fused-attn" did you mean the F-ATT path? The transcript earlier had it as "fused-atn" in the doc, just making sure it's the same variant.
[01:40] Ravi: Yes F-ATT. Sorry the auto-doc munged it.
[01:43] Hannah: Also worth noting that quantization profile A increases memory pressure which interacts poorly with long streaming sessions leading to GC-like stalls — the profiler traces show occasional memcpy stalls when KV cache gets warmed.
[02:05] Jonah: That matches what we saw — when multiple streams warmed the prefix cache it looked like network stalls, but NV counters showed GPU memcpy contention.
[02:22] Amir: Pause — can we clarify what you mean by prefix cache? Is that the request-side cache or KV cache in the model runtime? We mix terms.
[02:30] Ravi: Good call. We're using prefix/KV cache to mean the model-side KV store that holds past tokens for streaming sessions. It was sometimes transcribed as K V cash in earlier notes.
[02:42] Priya: Ok thanks. So on the streaming handshake issue — we saw ~3% of sessions get stuck in half-open state for 2–4s before timeout. The client retries cause duplicate sessions and increase microburst probability.
[03:05] Maya: Were those timeouts happening only on peak load?
[03:08] Priya: Mostly during our 1k concurrent microburst tests. At 1k concurrency with 40ms inter-arrival jitter we saw those half-open flows.
[03:20] Hannah: We captured pcap and NVTX traces; initial look shows the server-side backlog growth causing delayed accept() handling, then the stream state machine retries. This points to queueing at the kernel layer and thread scheduling.
[03:40] Ravi: So mitigation options — at the Redwood side we can change the accept backoff and increase ephemeral thread pool size which reduces the half-open window; second is to use a short pre-warm handshake for clients likely to stream.
[03:55] Leah: Pre-warm sounds heavy; can we do something client-side first? Like exponential backoff tweaks?
[04:02] Priya: We already tweaked client backoff, but the problem is the initial spike — many clients open concurrently. We need the server to absorb that.
[04:10] Maya: On TTFT we have two playbooks: 1) favor a fast fused kernel for median wins but risk tail spikes, 2) pick tiled/stable kernel for better tail but slightly worse median and cost. We need to map that to ParcelWave's success criteria.
[04:30] Amir: Our SLA is 350ms 95th — if fused gives median 80ms but 95th > 700 at microburst, that's not acceptable. We prefer stable 95th even if median is worse.
[04:45] Ravi: Understood. We'll propose kernel mapping where seqlen < 64 use the low-overhead fused path, seqlen 64–512 use tiled stable kernel, and >512 use streaming-optimized kernel with KV-level checkpointing. That's the initial matrix.
[05:05] Priya: For our typical distribution 70% of requests are <128 tokens, 25% 128–512, 5% >512. So the middle bucket is critical.
[05:20] Maya: We'll attach a matrix and also a fallback policy: if the server detects rising queue latency, switch to stable tiled kernel automatically per routing policy. That gives you guardrails.
[05:33] Jonah: How fast can that switch happen?
[05:35] Ravi: We can do per-node kernel hot-swap within ~2–7s depending on active KV handles — it's not instantaneous because we need to flush and rebuild certain caches.
[05:48] Priya: 2–7s still might create a few bad responses. Could we do a phased canary where we route 5% of traffic to tiled and monitor?
[05:58] Maya: Yes, canary is what we recommend. Proposed schedule — 5% for 24h, ramp to 20% if 24h looks good, then full flip in 48–72h.
[06:10] Amir: Sounds reasonable. Any security/VPC implications for canary on Dedicated?
[06:15] Maya: For Dedicated we can provision a small canary pool in your VPC or use Redwood-managed nodes with VPC peering. We'll send the options and the security checklist.
[06:26] Jonah: Network baseline — I'll pull egress numbers and also confirm our NAT gateway CPU during the microburst.
[06:33] Priya: Back to kernel selection — Ravi, can you explain the streaming-optimized kernel tradeoffs again?
[06:39] Ravi: Sure. The streaming kernel reduces per-token overhead by keeping an incremental work queue and amortizing KV lookups, but it assumes steady state. It has lower tail in steady streaming but higher cold-start TTFT because KV warming happens. So for chat-first experiences where you need fast initial response, it's tricky.
[07:01] Leah: That aligns with our UX priorities — initial reply must be snappy for user retention. We prefer better TTFT for first response even if later tokens are slower.
[07:12] Maya: We can support a hybrid: first token via fused path for snappy intro, then switch to streaming kernel for the remaining tokens. That's exactly our 'first-token fastpath' pattern.
[07:25] Priya: How does that work with KV? Does it duplicate KV load?
[07:28] Ravi: We snapshot the KV after first token and resume on streaming kernel; there's a small overhead but it avoids full cold start. It's been implemented in our pilot runs.
[07:39] Amir: Ok. On the microburst NVTX traces — Priya, what did you find?
[07:43] Priya: We saw spikes of memcpy and occasional GPU scheduler retrace. The interesting part was that when prefix cache warmed across multiple nodes we saw synchronized memcpy bursts — looks like a collective warm event.
[07:58] Hannah: Likely due to simultaneous cache eviction across shards — we need smarter eviction or staggered warm-up.
[08:05] Ravi: We have a couple of heuristics: staggered KV warming, lazy warming for lower probability tokens, and a soft cap on concurrent warm-up threads. We'll add that to the kernel matrix.
[08:18] Jonah: Also, can you quantify the cost impact? Because switching to tiled increases per-token GPU time and thus cost. We need a delta to show cost vs SLA.
[08:27] Maya: We'll include approximate unit economics — delta in GPU ms per token and projected monthly cost at your traffic profile.
[08:33] Amir: Good. On the canary, what metrics should we monitor?
[08:36] Ravi: TTFT median/95/99, streaming handshake fail rate, queue depth, GPU memcpy stalls, and end-to-end error rate. We'll provide a dashboard template.
[08:47] Priya: Also add 'first-byte jitter' — the variability in initial bytes for streaming.
[08:50] Hannah: We'll include NVTX and pcap links in the artifact.
[08:55] Maya: Action items recap: we'll send kernel matrix, cost delta, and canary schedule. ParcelWave runs microburst NVTX and provides egress baseline.
[09:05] Leah: Quick question on security posture — SSO and audit logs — we need to ensure audit log retention for 12 months. Does Redwood support that on Dedicated?
[09:15] Maya: Yes, Dedicated supports extended audit retention as an add-on; we'll include retention options and pricing.
[09:21] Jonah: Also need RBAC for team members; we don't want devs to flip kernels.
[09:25] Maya: RBAC support exists; we'll send role mapping suggestions.
[09:30] Amir: Anything else on the tech side?
[09:32] Priya: One nit — when you send the kernel matrix please call out which kernels are compatible with quant profile A vs B; earlier runs had mismatches.
[09:40] Ravi: Noted. We'll mark compatibility + memory footprint.
[09:44] Maya: Ok last bit — timeline. If we get the microburst traces and egress numbers early next week we can start a canary by 2026-04-25. Does that work?
[09:55] Amir: That's tight but doable.
[10:00] Priya: We'll prioritize the microburst NVTX run for 2026-04-18.
[10:03] Maya: Great — schedule followup 30-min on 2026-04-22 to confirm start and review artifacts.
[10:10] Jonah: One more question — competitors. We did mention OpenAI as a managed benchmark — are we considering any migration risk?
[10:16] Maya: We briefly discussed other providers; but our focus here is on cost/SLA tradeoffs. We'll include competitor notes as context.
[10:22] Amir: Thanks everyone.
[10:25] Maya: Thanks, I'll send the matrix and CSVs.
[10:29] (meeting ends)
